2121627795566567577.text:
3D harbour in the browser with Opus 5.5 + Blender + Three.js..

it started from a single drawing

matching the illustration first, then making it explorable. here’s the workflow:

- step 1: pick one illustration as the target, and lock the camera to its exact angle
- step 2: blender + mcp: have opus block out the stack from the drawing: pier, stilts, floors, stairs
- step 3: blender: opus builds the details in layers: rooftops > shopfronts > waterline > the stair
- step 4: blender: assign flat stylized materials, then export one glb
- step 5: three.js: opus loads the glb and adds teal water with ripples and reflections
- step 6: three.js: warm emissive windows, string lights and lanterns with bloom
- step 7: three.js: time of day toggles (dusk, day, rain, night) and drifting gulls
- step 8: three.js: camera modes: orbit, walk around the pier, steer the boat
- step 9: add the life: little robots wandering the piers and boats leaving wakes

if it doesn’t look right from the reference camera, it won’t look right anywhere

2122041787984613476.text:
I built Unreal Engine's Nanite System in threejs https://t.co/ySsY2v7wqp

Like Nanite in Unreal, you can drop in a film-quality mesh with millions of triangles as it is. No retopology, no decimating, no hand-made LODs. The engine works out how much of it to draw.

In the example below, there's 184 million triangles but only under 2 million are drawn without any meaningful dip in visual fidelity. 

How it works:

Every mesh is cut into small clusters of triangles, and each cluster is stored at many levels of detail. Every frame, each cluster picks the coarsest level that still looks identical at its size on screen. Close to the camera you get full detail; far away, a fraction of it.

Neighbouring clusters always agree on their shared edges, so there are no cracks and no popping.

You can also give the whole scene one triangle budget and it stays inside it. Hidden props are culled, and only the detail in view is streamed in.

What it doesn't have is Nanite's software rasteriser. WebGL2 has no compute shaders, so the win here comes from drawing far fewer triangles, not from making each one cheaper. WebGPU could do that part.

Works with stock three.js materials. It's open source with an MIT License. 

I wanted to experiment with it a bit more before posting about it but i thought it would be cool to set it free and see what others build with it and figure out better ways to optimize it in a communal manner! 

This is experimental so don't expect it to be as plug and play as it is inside unreal engine but it's still so cool to see how we can try out really interesting ideas in ways that were impossible only a few months ago.

2122041787984613476.post_text: Jemand hat das Nanite-Prinzip aus Unreal in three.js nachgebaut, Open Source unter MIT-Lizenz. Meshes werden in Cluster mit mehreren Detailstufen zerlegt, pro Frame wird nur so viel Detail gezeichnet, wie auf dem Bildschirm sichtbar ist. Im Beispiel sind es 184 Millionen Dreiecke, gezeichnet werden unter 2 Millionen. Für WebGL-Projekte mit schweren 3D-Assets finde ich das spannend, auch wenn der Autor es selbst noch experimentell nennt.
